## 🤖 AI & Tech
*Updated: 8:00 AM EST*

**India AI Impact Summit convenes the entire AI power structure in New Delhi—Altman, Pichai, Amodei, Hassabis under one roof signals India's geopolitical ambition**
The India AI Impact Summit (Feb 16-19, New Delhi, 250,000 expected visitors) is hosting the most concentrated gathering of AI leadership outside Silicon Valley: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis, and Reliance Chairman Mukesh Ambani—all in the same room. PM Modi is personally inaugurating the summit and chairing a CEO roundtable on Feb 19. India is explicitly positioning this as the "Global South's" response to the Paris AI Action Summit and the US-China AI race, framing itself as a third governance pole in AI's emerging multipolar order.

**Why this matters—India is transitioning from AI consumer to AI governance actor:** This isn't a tech conference; it's a geopolitical declaration. By assembling every major Western AI CEO plus India's industrial champion (Ambani/Reliance JioBrain), Modi signals that Indian market access, engineering talent, and regulatory frameworks are too significant to be dictated by Washington or Beijing. Every Western AI lab needs India's ~1.4B users, its world-class ML talent pipeline, and its data sovereignty regime to avoid EU-style fragmentation. In return, India gains technology partnerships, AI infrastructure investment, and a seat at the standard-setting table. The summit follows the AI Action Summit in Paris—the axis of AI governance is Paris → New Delhi → (Beijing/Washington sidelined)—which no one in Silicon Valley expected 18 months ago.

**ByteDance drops Seedance 2.0 + Doubao Seed 2.0 simultaneously—dual-front offensive in video and LLM races triggers Hollywood legal crisis**
ByteDance launched two major AI products within days of each other: Seedance 2.0 (text-to-video, image-to-video, 1080p cinematic quality, native synced audio) and Doubao Seed 2.0 (next-gen LLM with enhanced visual understanding). Seedance 2.0 immediately went viral by generating hyper-realistic footage of Tom Cruise fighting Brad Pitt—prompting Disney to file a cease and desist, the Motion Picture Association to formally denounce the model for copyright infringement, and NBC/NYT coverage treating it as genuine Hollywood emergency. ByteDance pledged to "strengthen current safeguards" under legal pressure.

**Why this is more than a copyright dispute—it's a test of whether AI video can be regulated:** Seedance 2.0's "physical accuracy, realism and controllability" is precisely why Hollywood panicked: the output is indistinguishable from real footage at typical social media resolution. Previous AI video (Sora, Runway, Kling) was detectable; Seedance 2.0 apparently isn't. The strategic play: ByteDance, already banned from US app stores via TikTok saga, has nothing to lose deploying via the open web. If Seedance 2.0 normalizes AI-generated deepfakes of real celebrities before legal frameworks exist, the precedent is catastrophic for talent rights. Disney's C&D is symbolic—no single studio can stop a Chinese tech giant distributing globally through API access. This requires either export controls on AI video models (unprecedented) or international IP treaty (impossible at current US-China relations temperature). Meanwhile, Doubao Seed 2.0's visual understanding improvements position ByteDance as serious LLM competitor, not just a consumer app company.

**AI-driven tech layoffs hit 30,700 in 2026 already—but "AI-washing" muddies the picture as companies exploit the narrative**
Layoffs.fyi data shows 30,700 tech roles eliminated in the first six weeks of 2026. AI was cited as a contributing factor in nearly 55,000 US layoffs throughout 2025. Amazon alone cut 16,000 jobs, framing it as a restructuring for an "AI future." Fox News reporting tech workers claiming AI has "completed their jobs"; UnHerd running a piece titled "The AI Jobs-Apocalypse Is Here." But here's the complication: analysts are flagging rampant "AI-washing" in layoff announcements—companies attributing cuts to AI automation when the real drivers are pandemic over-hiring unwind, margin pressure, and ordinary restructuring. NexaTech Ventures' Scott Dylan: "AI-washing is when companies blame AI for job cuts when the real drivers are far more mundane."

**Why the AI-washing signal is as important as the actual displacement:** Two competing realities are running in parallel. Reality 1: AI genuinely is replacing some white-collar tasks (customer support, entry-level coding, content moderation, data entry). Reality 2: corporations discovered that "AI replaced them" is less PR-damaging than "we over-hired and need to cut costs." The danger: inflated AI-layoff numbers create policy panic, potentially accelerating regulation that's poorly targeted. The actual labor displacement story is real but slower than headlines suggest—UnHerd notes AI is a "contributing factor" not the sole cause in most cases. For Freeze's job hunt: the AI/ML skills premium is real. Recruiters explicitly favor "hands-on AI projects and measurable business outcomes." The market bifurcation is AI-literate workers gaining leverage vs. AI-adjacent workers getting displaced.

**KPMG partner fined A$10,000 for using AI to cheat in mandatory AI training—over two dozen KPMG Australia staff caught since July**
A KPMG partner (senior rank) was fined A$10,000 by the firm for using AI to cheat during an internal training course *about* AI. This isn't an isolated incident—KPMG Australia confirmed 24+ staff have been caught doing the same since July 2025. The irony writes itself: people using AI to pass exams that certify they understand AI. But the signal is revealing—professional services firms mandating AI literacy training are discovering that their most senior, time-pressed employees treat compliance training as checkbox exercise rather than genuine upskilling.

**Why this exposes the gap between AI adoption narrative and ground truth:** Every Big 4 firm is publicly committed to "AI transformation." The reality: partners billable at £500-1,000/hour have zero incentive to spend 8 hours in mandatory e-learning. Cheating reveals that the training requirement exists for liability/optics, not genuine skill development. The actual AI capability in professional services concentrates among junior associates who learned these tools organically, while partners—who control client relationships and strategic decisions—remain AI-illiterate and hiding it. This creates a dangerous organizational inversion: the people making decisions about AI deployment don't understand what they're deploying, while the people who do understand it don't have decision authority.

**Tech companies accused of systematic greenwashing on AI climate claims—conflating traditional AI with generative AI to obscure energy costs**
A new report (The Guardian, Feb 17) finds tech companies are deliberately conflating traditional AI (optimization algorithms, predictive analytics—relatively energy-efficient) with generative AI (LLMs, image/video generation—massively energy-intensive) when claiming AI helps fight climate change. Energy analyst Ketan Joshi: the discourse "needs to be brought back to reality." The core deception: companies cite traditional AI's climate benefits (smart grid optimization, emissions monitoring) while simultaneously expanding energy-hungry generative AI workloads. Video generation and deep research functions are singled out as particularly egregious energy consumers being buried in the marketing narrative.

**The energy math is being hidden in plain sight:** Training a frontier LLM consumes megawatt-hours; video generation at scale consumes more per output than any previous AI application. Data center electricity demand is now projected to rival entire countries' national consumption by 2030. Regulators in EU, UK, and Australia are starting to probe AI energy disclosures specifically because companies are not treating generative AI and traditional AI as distinct categories. The implication for AI governance: if companies successfully conflate these categories, emissions accounting becomes impossible, climate commitments become meaningless, and the energy transition burden gets distributed across society while AI firms capture the productivity gains. The greenwashing allegation is serious—it's not "they overstated benefits" but "they systematically misrepresented which technology class they're referring to."

## 🌍 Geopolitics
*Updated: 8:15 AM EST*

**Geneva becomes the pivot of the world today — simultaneous Russia-Ukraine and US-Iran negotiations converge in one city, reshaping two crises at once**
Two of the most volatile conflicts on Earth are being negotiated under the same Swiss sky today. Round 3 of Russia-Ukraine-US talks begins Tuesday in Geneva, led by Ukraine's Rustem Umerov, Russia's Vladimir Medinsky (arch-conservative Putin adviser who has openly questioned Ukrainian sovereignty), and US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. Simultaneously, Witkoff and Kushner are scheduled for direct meetings with Iranian FM Abbas Araqchi in the same city—with Oman mediating—as Iran partially shut the Strait of Hormuz to signal leverage. The geographic collapse of two crisis tracks into one Swiss city is deliberate: it concentrates US diplomatic bandwidth (Witkoff/Kushner as the dual-wielding deal-closers of Trump's foreign policy), reduces travel overhead, and creates a media environment where "progress" on either front can be packaged as a Trump foreign policy win.

**Why Geneva's convergence is structurally significant:** This isn't diplomatic coincidence—it's a template. By co-locating the Ukraine and Iran tracks, Washington signals it sees both crises as transactional bargaining problems solvable by dealmakers rather than systemic security challenges requiring multilateral architecture. Russia broadened the Geneva scope beyond military ceasefire to "territorial questions and other demands"—Moscow is pushing maximalist positions (Peskov's framing) while Medinsky's presence (a man who wrote that Ukrainians and Russians are "one people") signals Russia still views this as a negotiation over Ukraine's political identity, not just its borders. Meanwhile, Iran shut part of Hormuz hours before talks—a classic escalation-to-negotiate move, showing Tehran's leverage window is the 20% of global oil transit it can threaten. Both crises share the same structural DNA: weaker party uses geography/chokepoints as leverage against a superpower distracted by domestic politics.

**UK and German defense chiefs issue unprecedented joint rearmament appeal—Europe is abandoning post-Cold War defense complacency in real time**
The heads of the British and German armed forces published a joint op-ed calling on European publics to accept the "moral" case for large-scale rearmament and prepare for potential war with Russia. This is historically unusual—joint appeals from two nuclear-adjacent militaries explicitly naming Russia as the threat and asking citizens to fund it through spending cuts elsewhere. The Munich Security Conference backdrop amplified the message: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz warned about US unilateralism, while US Secretary of State Marco Rubio reframed Washington's position as "adaptation" rather than abandonment of European security commitments.

**The transatlantic architecture is fracturing in productive ways:** The conventional framing is "NATO crisis"—but the more accurate read is European strategic emancipation accelerated by necessity. For 75 years, Europe free-rode on US security guarantees; Trump 2.0 is forcing a reckoning that German, French, and British establishments have resisted for decades. Merz calling for NATO-led coordination rather than unilateral action is significant—Germany's historically pacifist political culture is being rewritten in real time by a coalition chancellor who ran on a security-first platform. The UK-Germany joint appeal bypasses governments and speaks directly to publics because governments know the math: rearmament requires austerity elsewhere, and no European government wants to own that trade-off alone. Russia's response (Lavrov calling it "robbing taxpayers") is performative—Moscow's entire strategic calculus assumed European disunity would prevent rearmament. That assumption is now empirically wrong.

**Iran partially closes Strait of Hormuz + US-Iran nuclear talks resume in Geneva—energy markets and war risk are now the same variable**
Iran throttled traffic through the Strait of Hormuz (20% of global oil transit) hours before nuclear negotiations with US envoys began in Geneva. Simultaneously, Tehran signaled flexibility: Iran's FM indicated willingness to compromise on the nuclear programme in exchange for sanctions relief, with energy deals, mining contracts, and aircraft sales reportedly on the table. The US military has ramped up presence in the Middle East. Citi noted that China is buying Russian and Iranian oil at discounts for stockpiling, and expects this to continue as long as sanctions remain.

**The Hormuz gambit is Iran's only remaining leverage:** After losing Hamas as a proxy, Hezbollah as a forward deterrent, and Syria as a strategic corridor, Iran's bargaining position has shrunk to its geography. The Strait is the one card Tehran can't be stripped of without a full-scale war. By partially closing it *during* negotiations, Iran signals the floor of any deal: full sanctions relief must be on the table, not partial. The US military buildup is the counter-signal. What's new here is the scope of what's reportedly being discussed—not just nuclear caps, but energy investment, mining, and aircraft. This is less "JCPOA 2.0" and more a comprehensive normalization package, which would be the most significant US-Iran diplomatic reset since 1979. The obstacle: hardliners in both Tehran and Washington who benefit politically from perpetual confrontation. The window is narrow.

**OPEC+ signals April production increase as oil navigates supply glut vs. geopolitical premium**
Three OPEC+ sources told Reuters the alliance is leaning toward resuming output increases from April, capitalizing on summer demand expectations and current geopolitical price support. The backdrop: Western hemisphere production (US, Canada, Brazil) has surged, eroding OPEC+ market share; internal pressure from member states is mounting. Citi's analysis: geopolitics (Iran/Russia tensions) support near-term prices, but peace deals—if either the Ukraine or Iran track succeeds—would rapidly deflate the geopolitical premium baked into crude.

**The oil market is pricing two incompatible futures simultaneously:** A successful Geneva outcome (Ukraine ceasefire + Iran deal) would collapse the geopolitical risk premium and flood markets with previously-sanctioned Russian and Iranian supply—potentially a $15-20/barrel price shock. OPEC+ is threading a needle: increase production before a peace dividend removes their pricing power, but not so fast that they crash prices before the geopolitical floor disappears. The China factor compounds this—Beijing's discount buying of Russian/Iranian crude is a strategic stockpiling play, not just cost-cutting. If sanctions lift, China loses its preferred-buyer discount on ~10% of its oil imports. Energy geopolitics is more entangled than at any point since the 1973 embargo.
